text.p: Cambodia's economic growth is spurring a trend towards increased child labour in dangerous jobs, said a study released on Wednesday by a human rights organisation and a U.S. labour group.

The report, Child Labour in Cambodia, found that increasing investment and a growing demand for cheap labour were driving more children under 16 into hazardous work as factory and construction workers, drivers, stone cutters and salt field workers.

The report, issued by the Asian American Free Labor Institute (AAFLI), an affiliate of the AFL-CIO labour group, and Licadho, a local human rights organisation, was based on interviews with 245 working children in five provinces and Phnom Penh.
The release of the report came one day after the AFL-CIO, America's largest labour organisation, said it would oppose the extension of key trade benefits by the U.S. government to Cambodia.
The AFL-CIO said it opposed the concessions because of workers' rights abuses, including child labour.
A spokesman for the Labour Ministry was not available to comment.
Bama Athreya, AAFLI country representative, said she estimated more than half of Cambodia's estimated five million children under 16 worked, but noted that no updated statistics were available.
She said rights groups would continue to monitor the problem in hopes of promoting government action.
"The first step is getting the government to enforce the law. The second step will be getting these children a place to go," Athreya said.
An estimated 100 million children in Asia work full time, the report said.
